PixiJS 3D plays keyframe animation, both the clips in a glTF file and the animations you build in code. Most of the work goes through three classes: An Animation is a named set of keyframe tracks, such as a model's Walk clip. Each track drives one property, such as a bone's rotation or a node's position. A node is any Container3D in the scene. An AnimationPlayer plays animations on a node, such as a model, and on everything under it. An AnimationState is one animation's playback on one player: its time, speed, looping and weight. To move something in code every frame, such as a spinning coin, you don't need these classes. Change the node's transform from the ticker, as in 2D. Scene graph shows how.

A Model3D whose file has animation clips comes with a player, model.player. When the file has no clips, model.player is undefined. animationLabels lists the clips by name, and play starts one and returns its state: const fox = new Model3D({ source }); view3d.root.addChild(fox); const walk = fox.player!.play('Walk'); walk.animationSpeed = 1.5; play doesn't stop a clip that's already playing, so the two blend. To switch clips, call player.stop(), then play the next one. stop() stops every animation on the player, and each one holds its pose. Like an AnimatedSprite, a player advances on Ticker.shared. By default that isn't app.ticker, so slowing or pausing app.ticker doesn't affect the player. To drive the player from your own ticker, turn autoUpdate off and call update yourself: const fox = new Model3D({ source, autoUpdate: false }); app.ticker.add((ticker) => fox.player?.update(ticker));

getState returns an animation's state without starting playback. The state's methods match AnimatedSprite's, such as stop() and gotoAndPlay(), but they take times in seconds, not frame numbers. Setting time only moves the playhead. gotoAndStop(time) also shows the pose at that time straight away. loop is on by default. With it off, the state stops at its end, holds that pose and calls onComplete. To play it again, call gotoAndPlay(0). If a negative animationSpeed plays it backwards, call gotoAndPlay(state.animation.duration) instead. Here the walking fox stops, looks around once, then walks on: fox.player!.stop(); const survey = fox.player!.getState('Survey'); survey.loop = false; survey.onComplete = () => fox.player!.play('Walk'); survey.gotoAndPlay(0); Every model built from one source has its own player. Foxes in a crowd can each set a different time on their walk state, so they walk out of step.

All playing states apply at once. Where two states drive a property through tracks with the same label, as a model's clips do, the player mixes them by weight. Weights are relative. A clip that is the only one driving a property shows in full at any weight above 0, so lowering its weight doesn't fade it out. To fade it out, move weight to another clip. A track you write for one of a model's bones or nodes doesn't mix with the file's clips. Add to the clip's pose instead, as Skinned meshes shows. To crossfade, move the weights a step each frame, toward 1 on the clip you want and toward 0 on the other. One ticker callback then fades either way, even when you switch partway through a fade: const player = fox.player!; const walk = player.play('Walk'); const run = player.getState('Run'); let target = walk; app.ticker.add((ticker) => { const step = ticker.deltaMS / 300; for (const state of [walk, run]) { state.weight = state === target ? Math.min(1, state.weight + step) : Math.max(0, state.weight - step); if (state.weight === 0) state.stop(); } }); const fadeTo = (next: AnimationState) => { if (!next.playing) { next.weight = 0; next.play(); } target = next; }; button.on('pointertap', () => fadeTo(target === walk ? run : walk)); A stopped state keeps its weight, so the snippet sets a stopped clip's weight to 0 before playing it. While the ticker callback runs, it sets both weights, so switch clips by changing its target, as the button does. Once you remove the callback, set a faded-out clip's weight above 0 before you play it again, or the clip has no effect. Two looping clips that start on the same foot and step in the same order can begin the fade in step. Start the incoming clip at the same fraction of its duration that the outgoing clip has reached, by setting its time before you play it. The fox's walk and run don't line up this way. Playing clips crossfades the fox between its clips and blends its walk with its run.

A skinned mesh bends with a skeleton. A skeleton is a hierarchy of bones, such as a character's spine and limbs, and each bone moves the vertices tied to it. A Model3D lists its skeletons in model.skeletons. Every model gets its own, so posing one fox doesn't move another. getChildByLabel finds only the bones that the file puts a mesh under, as Scene graph explains. You move those like any node. The other bones exist only in the skeleton. indexOf finds a bone by its name in the file, and the skeleton keeps each bone's local position, rotation and scale in flat arrays. localRotation holds each bone's rotation as a quaternion, four numbers per bone. Write into the arrays and set dirty, or call setLocalTRS, which does both. A playing clip rewrites the bones it drives on every update, so a pose you write to those bones lasts only until the next update. To add to a clip's pose, turn the model's autoUpdate off so you choose the order, then pose the bone right after you update the player: const fox = new Model3D({ source, autoUpdate: false, autoPlay: 'Walk' }); const skeleton = fox.skeletons[0]; const head = skeleton.indexOf('b_Head_05') * 4; const turn = new Quaternion().setFromAxisAngle({ x: 0, y: 1, z: 0 }, Math.PI / 6); const rotation = new Quaternion(); view3d.root.addChild(fox); app.ticker.add((ticker) => { fox.player!.update(ticker); // Turn the head a further 30 degrees, on top of the pose the walk just set rotation.fromArray(skeleton.localRotation, head).multiply(turn).toArray(skeleton.localRotation, head); skeleton.dirty = true; }); While the walk plays, it resets the head on every update, so the turn doesn't build up. Once no playing clip drives the bone, as after player.stop(), write the whole rotation instead of multiplying onto the current one, or the head turns further every frame. A bone turns about its own axes, which depend on how the file was rigged, so check the axis on your model. Driving bones turns the fox's head toward the pointer the same way. Picking and culling don't follow the bones. For an animated character's hit volume, see Interaction. For a character that vanishes near the screen's edge, see Performance.

A morph target is another shape stored for the same vertices, such as a smile or a blink. A mesh whose geometry has morph targets has weights, one number per target. At 0 the mesh keeps its base shape, at 1 it takes the target's shape, and several targets add together. Clips in the file can drive the weights, or you can set them yourself: model.traverse((node) => { if (node instanceof Mesh3D && node.weights) node.weights[0] = 0.8; }); Write into the array rather than assigning a new one, because a clip that has started keeps using the old array. Each model has its own weights, even when several models share one source. Morph targets from glTF plays a cube's clip on its weights. A playing clip rewrites the weights on every update, so the example stops the clip when you set a weight by hand.

To animate a node's properties in code, such as its position or a mesh's weights, build an Animation from tracks. Each track names the property it drives as '<node label>.<property>' and holds keyframe times in seconds, with a value for each: const crate = new Mesh3D({ geometry: new CubeGeometry(), material: new Material3D(), label: 'crate', parent: view3d.root, }); const bob = new Animation({ label: 'bob', tracks: [new NumberTrack({ label: 'crate.y', times: [0, 0.5, 1], values: [0, 1, 0] })], }); const player = new AnimationPlayer({ target: crate, animations: [bob], autoPlay: 'bob' }); The player looks under its target for each track's node by label, or for a skinned mesh's bone by name, as TrackOptions.label describes. It looks each label up once, the first time an animation that uses it plays or you call gotoAndStop on its state, so add the nodes before then. A track that names no node, or a property the player can't animate, does nothing and gives no warning. A track can't reach a material, and among nodes only a Sprite3D has an alpha. When copies under one target share a label, only one of them animates, so give each copy its own player. Players can share one animation. Pick the track class by the property's type: Track Property Numbers per value Vector3Track A vector, such as position, scale, or rotation in radians 3 QuaternionTrack quaternion 4 NumberTrack A number, such as y 1 Track An array of numbers, such as weights, with valueSize valueSize A position track sets all three coordinates. To keep the x and z you placed the node at, animate y alone with a NumberTrack. A rotation track also sets all three angles, so use a Vector3Track even to turn about one axis. angle doesn't animate. On a bone, a track drives only position, quaternion or scale, so turn a bone with a QuaternionTrack. interpolation sets how a track fills in values between keyframes. With 'CUBICSPLINE', each keyframe stores two tangents beside its value, in the layout TrackOptions.values describes. With 'LINEAR' interpolation, the default, a QuaternionTrack turns the shorter way between two keyframes, so keep each step under half a turn. A Vector3Track on rotation turns through the angles as you give them. An animation ends at its last keyframe. To hold the end pose before it loops, set a longer duration. Keyframes assembles the PixiJS logo with a Vector3Track for each piece. A QuaternionTrack rolls its badge and a NumberTrack flashes a light. The example plays the same keyframes with each interpolation.

A model's destroy also destroys its player and skeletons. A player you built isn't tied to its target. If it's playing when you destroy the target, it keeps running on Ticker.shared, so call its destroy too. Also remove the ticker callbacks you added to drive a player or its bones, such as the crossfade and the head turn above.
Loading models: where models and their clips come from. Scene graph and transforms: how a node's rotation and quaternion relate, and which one the node uses.

A ContainerTexture draws a PixiJS Container into a texture, and a material shows that texture the same way it shows an image. That puts 2D content on a 3D surface, such as a score board over a shooting gallery: import { ContainerTexture, FlatMaterial, Mesh3D, PlaneGeometry } from '@pixi/3d'; import { Container, Graphics, Text } from 'pixi.js'; const board = new Container(); const digits = new Text({ text: '0', anchor: 0.5, style: { fontSize: 80, fontWeight: '800', fill: 0xffc46b } }); digits.position.set(256, 64); board.addChild(new Graphics().rect(0, 0, 512, 128).fill(0x1b1430), digits); const texture = new ContainerTexture({ container: board, width: 512, height: 128, renderer: app.renderer }); const sign = new Mesh3D({ geometry: new PlaneGeometry({ width: 2.4, height: 0.6 }), material: new FlatMaterial({ baseColorTexture: texture }), }); view3d.root.addChild(sign); The texture stretches over the whole plane, so give the plane the board's shape. The plane's 2.4 by 0.6 is the board's 512 by 128 scaled down. FlatMaterial ignores the scene's lights, so the board looks lit from within, like a screen. A lit Material3D shades it like a poster on a wall. Container texture uses this to put a bouncing PixiJS wordmark and a clock on a monitor's screen.

The texture takes the container out of any parent it had, so the container no longer draws on the stage. Adding it back to the stage takes it out of the texture, which then captures nothing. To show the same content in 2D as well, build it twice, or show the texture in a sprite. width and height set the area the texture captures. That's the rectangle from (0, 0) to (width, height), as if the container sat on the stage of a canvas that size. Leave both out and the texture sizes itself to the container's contents, measured once when you create it. That works only when the container's own transform, such as its position or scale, is at its defaults. For any other container, give the size. A Text with no resolution of its own draws at the renderer's resolution, whatever the texture's resolution is. Give the texture resolution: app.renderer.resolution so the two match. antialias smooths the edges of 2D shapes drawn into the texture. The application's antialias option doesn't apply to them.

An opaque material, the default alphaMode, draws the container's empty parts black and turns the soft edges next to them hard. To keep those edges smooth, fill the container's background, as the board above does, or set clearColor to 'black'. For gaps you can see through, such as rounded corners, use alphaMode: 'blend'.

The texture doesn't redraw itself unless you turn on autoUpdate, described below. With a renderer, the texture draws once when you create it, unless you turn firstRender off. Without one, it stays empty until its first render, and an opaque material shows it black. The texture keeps the renderer you give it, in its options or in a render call, so later calls can leave it out. When the content changes. A score or a health bar changes far less often than every frame, so render the texture after each change. In between, the surface keeps the last picture and nothing draws the 2D content again: function setScore(points: number): void { digits.text = String(points); texture.render(); } Every frame. For content that animates all the time, call render from app.ticker after you change the container. A callback added to app.ticker runs before the application draws, so the surface shows this frame's picture: app.ticker.add(() => { readout.text = (performance.now() / 1000).toFixed(1); texture.render(app.renderer); }); Container texture has a setting that switches between the two. Set to render on change, it renders only when its clock's seconds change, so the bouncing wordmark on the screen falls behind and catches up once a second. autoUpdate renders the texture every frame from Ticker.shared, once it has a renderer. A default Application draws from a ticker of its own, so the surface shows the previous frame's capture. To show the capture in the same frame, create the application with sharedTicker: true, or call render from app.ticker as above. Call render before the application draws. Never call it from code that runs during a render, such as an onRender callback. setContainer makes a texture capture another container. The texture keeps its size and GPU memory, so one screen can switch between menus. Render the texture after the switch.

The container isn't on the stage, so pointer events never reach its children. Listen on the mesh instead. With hitVolume set to 'geometry', a pointer event's e.hit3D holds uv, the mesh's own texture coordinate under the pointer, as Interaction shows. It's the coordinate before the material's uvTransform or a texture's frame changes it. On the board above, which has neither, the point in the capture is (uv.x * width, (1 - uv.y) * height). On a glTF mesh flipped as shown below, it's (uv.x * width, uv.y * height).

The texture stores the container's bottom row first, the other way up from an image. On a plane without flipV, it shows upright, like the board above. Geometry says how each built-in shape shows it. On a loaded model's mesh, such as a screen in a glTF room, it shows upside down, because glTF starts its texture coordinates at an image's top row. Flip v, the vertical texture coordinate, with the mesh material's uvTransform, as the crate in Geometry does. This flip and the click point above both need texture coordinates stored as floats, which gltfpack doesn't keep by default. Mesh quantization says why. A 2D Sprite shows it upside down as well, so flip the sprite: import { Sprite } from 'pixi.js'; const preview = new Sprite(texture); preview.anchor.y = 1; preview.scale.y = -1; // upright, in the place an unflipped sprite would take A Sprite3D shows it upside down too, and Sprite3D says what to use instead.

A ContainerSource is the source behind a ContainerTexture. Build one yourself to cut several textures from one container with frames, as from a sprite sheet. One render of the source updates them all. Because the bottom row comes first, a frame's y counts up from the container's bottom edge: import { ContainerSource } from '@pixi/3d'; import { Rectangle, Texture } from 'pixi.js'; // icons is 256 by 256, with two 128-pixel icons along its top const sheet = new ContainerSource({ container: icons, width: 256, height: 256, renderer: app.renderer }); const play = new Texture({ source: sheet, frame: new Rectangle(0, 128, 128, 128) }); // top left const pause = new Texture({ source: sheet, frame: new Rectangle(128, 128, 128, 128) }); // top right

A View3D is a 2D display object, so it can go in the container, and the texture then shows its 3D scene. To nest one scene inside another: Size the view to the texture with width and height, not autoResize, which sizes a view to the canvas even inside a texture. The picture already includes the inner scene's lighting, so show it with a FlatMaterial, which doesn't light it again. Render the innermost texture first, so each texture captures the latest picture of the ones inside it. A texture can't appear inside the container it captures, so give each level its own texture. For a second angle on the same scene, such as a security monitor, use a second camera instead, as Second cameras shows.

destroy() leaves the texture's ContainerSource alive, and if autoUpdate is on, the source keeps rendering every frame. destroy(true) frees the source and its GPU memory and stops autoUpdate. Either way the container survives, unless you pass { container: true }, which destroys the container and its children along with the source. texture.destroy(true); Destroying a material with texture: true destroys the texture but leaves its source alive in the same way. Add textureSource: true to free the source too. Destroy3DOptions says how a mesh passes these flags to its material.
View3D and 2D content: the other way to mix 2D into a scene, a 2D label pinned over a 3D object. Materials: the alpha modes that decide what the texture's empty parts show.

@pixi/3d/extras has a few tools that show what a scene holds and how a view draws it. Use them while you work on a scene, and leave them out of what you ship. logHierarchy prints a container and everything under it to the console, one line each, with its class and label. Use it to see what a loaded model holds. Loading models says how a file's names become labels, and Parents and children shows how getChildByLabel finds one. If you load PixiJS 3D from the CDN, map dist/pixijs-3d.mjs and dist/pixijs-3d-extras.mjs while you debug. Class names then print in full, both in the console and in the overlay below.

WireframePass is a pass, one of the steps a view takes to draw a frame. It draws meshes a second time as lines, over their shading, so you can see how many triangles a mesh has and where they go. Add the pass to the view, then opt meshes in by its name, 'wireframe', as with any mesh pass. Use a material's passes option, or enablePass to opt in one mesh at a time, as Passes per mesh does with outlines. A Model3D has no enablePass, so walk a loaded model with traverse to reach its meshes: import { Mesh3D } from '@pixi/3d'; import { WireframePass } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; view3d.passes = [...view3d.passes, new WireframePass({ color: 0x00ff88 })]; model.traverse((node) => { if (node instanceof Mesh3D) node.enablePass('wireframe'); }); Outlines and wireframes turns the pass on and off over a puck, a sphere and a torus. The lines show through whatever is in front of them, including the far side of the mesh. They aren't an exact wireframe. Some edges are missing, and some lines aren't edges at all. Leave out meshes whose geometry has no normals, the direction each vertex faces, such as the fox from the Quick start. Rendering throws on them, and the app stops drawing.

GraphDebugOverlay is an HTML panel that records how a view draws each frame. Create it with the view and the renderer: import { GraphDebugOverlay } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; new GraphDebugOverlay({ view: view3d, renderer: app.renderer }); The panel sits in the top-right corner of the page. Once the view has rendered, press Record, use your app, then press Stop. A recording also stops by itself after maxRecordedFrames frames. Recording adds CPU time to each frame, so stop it before you measure frame times. After you press Stop, the panel fills most of the window, with a slider that steps through the recorded frames. Hide shrinks it to a button. The panel has two tabs: Workload covers each pass that draws meshes, such as the shadow, opaque or wireframe pass. It shows each pass's draws and triangles, and how its draws compare with the frame before: reused, repacked or rebuilt (GraphDebugDrawBuildSnapshot.status lists them all). Select a pass, then a row. A pass has one row for the scene's meshes and one for each BatchedMesh3D. The Inspector says why the draws changed and lists them. Select a draw to see its meshes, materials, textures and geometry. ‹ Change and Change › skip to frames where a pass did extra work, such as rebuilding its draws. Render Graph lists every pass the view built, including the ones it skipped that frame, with the textures each one reads and writes. How a frame renders explains the passes. The Inspector lists a draw's meshes by label, so give your meshes one. Three things to look for in Workload: More draws than you expect. The row's Geo, Mat and Tex columns count the geometries, materials and textures its draws use. What makes a draw call explains which meshes can share one. Draws rebuilt on frames where nothing should change. The Inspector names the cause, such as a geometry or material change, and GraphDebugDrawRebuildCauseCode lists every cause. In the transparent pass, expect order changed while the camera moves. Meshes with alphaMode: 'blend' draw back to front, so the view sorts them again. mesh added or mesh removed on every frame. Adding or removing a mesh repacks or rebuilds the draws. Hide the mesh with visible instead, and the view reuses the draws. Copy Frame copies the frame you're looking at to the clipboard as JSON. Copy Recording copies every recorded frame, in the shape GraphDebugRecording.toJSON returns. destroy removes the panel.

VelocityViewer replaces the picture with how far each pixel's surface moved on screen since the last frame. That motion is what MotionBlurEffect blurs by. The hue shows the direction and the brightness shows the speed, and the class reference lists the colours. Like the blur, it sees only the camera's motion, so with the camera still the picture is black, even where objects move. import { VelocityViewer } from '@pixi/3d/extras'; const viewer = new VelocityViewer({ scale: 0.6 }); view3d.passes = [...view3d.passes, viewer]; // it replaces the picture, so it goes last window.addEventListener('keydown', (e) => { if (e.key === 'v') viewer.enabled = !viewer.enabled; }); Raise scale to brighten slow motion. In Motion blur, an inset shows the orbiting scene through a VelocityViewer, beside the blur that follows the same motion.
Performance: what puts meshes in one draw call, and a checklist for phones. How a frame renders: the passes the overlay lists, in the order they run.

A DirectionalLight lights a scene from one direction. Real places also get light from everywhere else, such as the sky, the ground and the walls of a room. The view's environment adds that light from all around, and it's what shiny surfaces reflect. That light casts no shadows, not even from a sun in a photo of the sky, so add a DirectionalLight with castShadow for those. Material3D, the material most glTF models load with, takes both its light and its reflections from the environment. PhongMaterial takes its light from it but doesn't reflect it, and FlatMaterial ignores it. A view has no environment by default, so a metal looks dark apart from its highlights. An AmbientLight doesn't brighten it either, as Lights explains. Environment light lights a metal PixiJS logo from nothing but its environment, and switches that environment between a cube map, a sky and ground gradient, and a single colour.

A Hemisphere is the simplest environment. It holds a sky colour and a ground colour. A surface facing up takes the sky colour, one facing down takes the ground colour, and the sides blend the two. It needs no image and costs less to draw than a cube map, as the checklist for phones notes. The view reads the object every frame, so keep a reference to it and change its colours or intensity at any time, for example to fade from day to dusk: import type { Hemisphere } from '@pixi/3d'; const sky: Hemisphere = { skyColor: 0x8ec5ff, groundColor: 0x8a6a4a }; view3d.environment = sky; // Later, at dusk sky.skyColor = 0xff8f6b; sky.groundColor = 0x3a2a55; sky.intensity = 0.8;

A cube map is six square images of the surroundings, one for each side of a cube around the scene. Lighting a scene from one is called image-based lighting, or IBL. Surfaces pick up the colours around them. Shiny ones also reflect a picture of the place, sharp on a smooth surface and blurred on a rough one. @pixi/3d adds a loader to Assets for .cubemap files, which list the six images: import { Assets } from 'pixi.js'; import type { CubeTexture } from 'pixi.js'; const sunset = await Assets.load<CubeTexture>('https://pixijs.com/assets/3d/venice-sunset/venice-sunset.cubemap'); view3d.environment = sunset; Environment light lights a metal PixiJS logo with this cube map. The logo sits between a chrome ball that shows the cube map's reflections and a matte ball that shows its soft light. On the first frame that lights a scene with a cube map, PixiJS 3D makes a copy of it for lighting and reflections to read. The copy is at most 256 pixels wide per face, so faces wider than 256 pixels sharpen the background but not the reflections. Making the copy takes GPU time once for each cube map, as How a frame renders notes. On WebGL2 the copy needs the EXT_color_buffer_float extension, and rendering throws on a device without it. WebGL and WebGPU covers such devices.

A .cubemap file is JSON that names an image for each face, with paths relative to the file: { "right": "px.jpg", "left": "nx.jpg", "top": "py.jpg", "bottom": "ny.jpg", "front": "pz.jpg", "back": "nz.jpg" } right, top and front are the +X, +Y and +Z sides. A camera looking down -Z, as the default camera does, sees back straight ahead. A JPG sky stops at white, so its sun is no brighter than a white cloud. A Radiance .hdr panorama keeps light brighter than white, and sites such as Poly Haven publish their skies in that format. A JPG panorama loads as a flat texture, which environment doesn't take, but Assets.load turns an .hdr panorama into a cube map: const sky = await Assets.load<CubeTexture>('venice_sunset_1k.hdr'); view3d.environment = sky; view3d.background = sky; The conversion runs on the main thread while the file loads, so the page freezes for a moment. loadHdr gives timings. HDR environment splits the screen between the Venice sunset as an .hdr and the same sunset as a .cubemap of six JPGs, with a metal logo in each half. Both halves start two stops darker, at a quarter of the light. The .hdr sun still shows as a bright glint in the metal, and the JPG sun has turned grey. Destroying a view, or switching it to another environment, doesn't free a cube map or its copy. To free a cube map you loaded, call Assets.unload with its URL once no view uses it, such as after you destroy the view. If it was a background you replaced, wait until the view has drawn a frame with another background that isn't null. Unloading frees the cube map, its images and the copy: await Assets.unload('https://pixijs.com/assets/3d/venice-sunset/venice-sunset.cubemap');

background draws behind the scene. It takes a cube map, a sky and ground gradient, or a plain colour. With none, the default, the 2D content behind the view shows through, as View3D describes. Give it the same object as the environment, and the sky you see matches the light on the scene. The two can also differ. This view lights its model with the sunset but draws a dark gradient behind it, so the model stands out: const view3d = new View3D({ autoResize: true, environment: sunset, background: { skyColor: 0x2b2738, groundColor: 0x0d0c12 }, }); The background is infinitely far away, so moving the camera never changes it, but turning the camera shows another part of it. With an orthographic camera, one where nothing shrinks with distance, leave it null and give the app a background colour instead.

Lighting can make a colour brighter than the screen's white. toneMapping decides how the view turns the scene's light into screen colours. Under the default, 'none', anything brighter than white clips. At an exposure of 1, a colour you give a FlatMaterial, a Sprite3D or a plain background then draws exactly as it would in 2D. A filmic curve such as 'aces' instead eases bright light toward white. It changes other colours too, unlit ones included, so a white background draws light grey. ToneMapping lists the curves. Use a curve for a scene lit by a bright sky or strong lights, and keep 'none' where the 3D should match your 2D art. Changing it later can stall a frame while new shaders compile, as How a frame renders explains, so set it when you create the view. exposure multiplies the scene's light, background and fog included, before the tone mapping curve. It's free to change every frame. Photographers count exposure in stops, where each stop doubles the light: view3d.exposure = 2 ** stops; // -1 halves the light, +1 doubles it

fog fades surfaces toward a colour the farther they are in front of the camera, which hides where the scene ends. Fog doesn't apply to the background, so give the background the same colour. Surfaces in full fog then match it with no visible edge, whatever the tone mapping and exposure. Fog distances count from the camera, so set them from how far the camera is from what it frames: const view3d = new View3D({ autoResize: true, background: 0x14131c, fog: { type: 'linear', color: 0x14131c, near: distance, far: distance + 12 }, }); The app's own background colour matches the fog only under the default tone mapping at an exposure of 1. Fog also fades the model once it's farther than near in front of the camera. To keep it off the model with an OrbitCamera that zooms out, set near beyond its maxDistance plus the model's radius. A floor's edge stays visible unless it's beyond far wherever the camera goes. The farther away the fade starts, the thinner the strip it fills at the horizon. A floor much brighter or darker than the fog then ends in a hard band, so give the fog a colour close to the floor's lit colour. type picks a FogType. 'linear', the default, runs from no fog at near to full fog at far. 'exponential' and 'exp2' thicken at a rate set by density instead. Density is 0 by default, so set it, or these curves show no fog. The view keeps the object you assign, so changing its colour or distances later is free. Its type is read-only, so assign a new object to switch curves, or null to turn fog off. Turning fog on or off, or switching its curve, can stall a frame while shaders compile, just as a tone mapping change can. A material created with fog set to false ignores the fog.

Lights: the direct lights that work alongside an environment. PBR materials: how metalness and roughness decide what a surface reflects. Post-processing: effects such as bloom, which work on the scene's light before tone mapping.

3D nodes, the counterpart of 2D containers, take PixiJS's own pointer events. Set a node's eventMode and listen on it as you would on a 2D container. The event names, the capture and bubble phases and cursor are the same. const button = new Mesh3D({ geometry: new CubeGeometry(), material: new Material3D({ baseColor: 0x3399ff }) }); view3d.root.addChild(button); button.eventMode = 'static'; button.cursor = 'pointer'; button.on('pointertap', () => console.log('clicked the cube')); To PixiJS, a View3D is one 2D object. When the pointer is over it, the view casts a ray, a line from the camera through the pointer, into the scene. It finds the closest node the ray hits and sends the event to that node through its 3D parents. Finding that node is called picking. Pointer events shows hover, taps and the mouse wheel on 3D shapes.

eventMode takes the same values as in 2D, and every 3D node starts as 'passive': 'static': the view hit-tests the node, and the node fires its listeners. 'dynamic': like 'static', and the view also tests again while the mouse or pen stays still, so a node that moves under the pointer gets its enter and leave events. 'passive': the node fires no listeners. Under an interactive ancestor, the view still hit-tests it and sends the hit to that ancestor. So setting a model or group to 'static' makes every mesh in it clickable. 'none': picking skips the node and everything under it. The renderer's eventMode option sets the default only for 2D containers, so 3D nodes stay 'passive' until you set them. Each pick tests every node that takes part, so set the mode only on the nodes and groups that need it.

The view hit-tests a node against its hitVolume, the 3D version of hitArea. Left unset, a Mesh3D uses its geometry's bounding box, the smallest box that holds all its vertices. A plain Container3D has no shape of its own, so it gets events only through its children. mesh.hitVolume = 'box'; // the bounding box, the default for a mesh mesh.hitVolume = 'geometry'; // every triangle mesh.hitVolume = new Sphere(new Vector3(0, 0, 0), 0.5); // a shape you choose, in the node's own space mesh.hitVolume = new CapsuleGeometry(); // a simpler stand-in mesh, tested per triangle The bounding box is cheap, but around a round object its empty corners count as hits. 'geometry' is exact, but its cost grows with the triangle count. A Box or Sphere you make can fit the object better, and is as cheap to test as the bounding box. Hit volumes outlines each shape's volume and lets you switch it. Per-triangle tests only work on ordinary triangle meshes with float positions. By default, gltfpack quantizes a model's positions to integers. Such a model never hits per triangle, so give it the bounding box or a stand-in. HitVolume3DInput lists the other limits. Skinning and morph targets are the ways a model changes shape as it animates. Picking reads a mesh's vertices as stored, so neither one moves what the ray hits or the default bounding box. Give an animated character a Box or Sphere that covers it in every pose. A Sprite3D, like any mesh whose billboardMode isn't 'none', turns to face the camera only when it's drawn. Picking still tests the unturned quad, which thins to an edge when seen from the side. Give it a Sphere too. A sphere set on a Sprite3D itself comes out squashed or stretched, so put the sphere on a group that holds the sprite instead. Set the group's interactiveChildren to false as below, and listen on the group. Setting interactiveChildren to false takes everything below a node out of picking, so the view tests the node's own hit volume in place of its children's. One box on a group then covers all its meshes, with one test instead of one per mesh: target.eventMode = 'static'; target.hitVolume = 'box'; // on a group, it fits around the children once, when you set it target.interactiveChildren = false;

A pointer listener on a 3D node gets a Pointer3DEvent, PixiJS's own event object with three Event3DFields added: hit3D: what the ray hit, as a RaycastHit3D, or null on a miss. Its point is in world space, the scene's own coordinates. A per-triangle hit also has the normal, the direction the surface faces, and uv, the texture coordinate under the pointer. Box and sphere hits report zeros for both. On a model whose texture coordinates are quantized, stored as integers, uv holds the hit's place in its triangle instead, so the painting below doesn't work there. target3D: the 3D node the event is about. That's usually the node the ray hit or, when that node is 'passive', its nearest interactive ancestor. To find which mesh of a model the ray hit, set the meshes to 'static' too and listen on the model. target3D is then the mesh. currentTarget3D: the node whose listeners are running now. With uv, painting on a mesh takes a few lines. Here the mesh shows a canvas as its texture, and each move with a button or finger down draws into it: easel.eventMode = 'static'; easel.hitVolume = 'geometry'; easel.on('pointermove', (e) => { if (!e.hit3D || !e.buttons) return; context.fillRect(e.hit3D.uv.x * canvas.width, e.hit3D.uv.y * canvas.height, 8, 8); texture.source.update(); }); Painting on a mesh paints a ball this way. It sends the canvas to the GPU at most once a frame rather than on every move. PixiJS reuses event objects, so hit3D and its vectors change with the next event. Copy any value you keep, as in saved.copyFrom(e.hit3D.point).

An event travels through the 3D hierarchy the same way it does through the 2D one. Capture listeners such as pointerdowncapture run on the way down, and plain listeners run on the way back up. As in 2D, an on* handler property runs in every phase that reaches the node, so a parent's onpointerdown runs twice per event. Event propagation logs every node a press reaches on its way through a table, a tray and the shapes on the tray, and lets you choose which listener calls stopPropagation(). stopPropagation() stops the event at the current node, and the view's plain on() listeners don't get it either. An OrbitCamera listens on the view, so stopping a press on an object keeps the drag from turning the camera, as Dragging shows. Plain view3d.on() listeners run after the 3D listeners and can read the 3D fields. On empty space, target3D is null. The view takes pointer events by default, so you don't need to set its eventMode.

These work as in 2D: A press and release on the same node counts as a tap, however far the pointer moved. So a drag that orbits the camera and ends on the view taps the view. It taps the model too when it started and ended on one. A hovered node that you remove from the scene, or set to 'passive' or 'none', gets no pointerout or pointerleave. Reset its hover look when you remove or disable it. To act only on real clicks, ignore a tap that ends more than a few pixels from where the press began. These listeners on the view do that and select the clicked node, or nothing on empty space: const pressedAt = new Point(); view3d.on('pointerdowncapture', (e) => pressedAt.copyFrom(e.global)); // runs even when a 3D listener stops the press view3d.on('pointertap', (e) => { if (Math.hypot(e.global.x - pressedAt.x, e.global.y - pressedAt.y) > 8) return; // the user dragged the camera select(e.target3D); // null on empty space }); Only the target's cursor counts, so set it on the node that becomes target3D, even when your listener is on the view. Over empty space, and over a target without one, the view's own cursor shows. A Mesh3D takes its colour from its material, so show hover and selection there: swap materials, set baseColor on a material only that mesh uses, or outline it. A model's meshes share their materials with every model built from the same file, so setting baseColor on one of those materials changes every model. To highlight one of a model's meshes, copy its material once with clone, such as mesh.material.clone({ baseColor: 0xffe08a }), and swap the mesh to the copy and back. The copy keeps the mesh's textures.

A drag has to keep going after the pointer leaves the object, so listen for globalpointermove, which fires on every move anywhere on the page. Add the listener when the drag starts, and remove it on both pointerup and pointerupoutside. The node you pressed gets pointerupoutside when you release anywhere else. Each finger on a touch screen is its own pointer, so compare pointerId to keep two drags apart. e.global is still the pointer's 2D position. To slide a crate across the floor, use screenToWorld to find where the pointer's ray meets the floor's Plane. Keep the crate's offset from the point you grabbed: const floor = new Plane(new Vector3(0, 1, 0), 0); const point = new Vector3(); crate.eventMode = 'static'; crate.on('pointerdown', (e) => { e.stopPropagation(); // an orbit camera on the view never sees this press if (!view3d.screenToWorld(e.global, floor, point)) return; const id = e.pointerId; // e is reused, so copy what the listeners below need const dx = crate.position.x - point.x; const dz = crate.position.z - point.z; const onMove = (move: Pointer3DEvent): void => { if (move.pointerId === id && view3d.screenToWorld(move.global, floor, point)) { crate.position.set(point.x + dx, crate.position.y, point.z + dz); } }; const onEnd = (end: Pointer3DEvent): void => { if (end.pointerId !== id) return; crate.off('globalpointermove', onMove); crate.off('pointerup', onEnd); crate.off('pointerupoutside', onEnd); }; crate.on('globalpointermove', onMove); crate.on('pointerup', onEnd); crate.on('pointerupoutside', onEnd); }); Dragging objects drags shapes across a level plane, holding each by the point you grab.

raycast casts the same ray through any point in global coordinates and returns the closest hit, without an event. Use it where no pointer event gives you the point, such as aiming from the middle of the screen in a first-person game. Pass it a hit from createRaycastHit3D to fill, so a pick on every frame makes no garbage: const aim = createRaycastHit3D(); const middle = { x: 0, y: 0 }; app.ticker.add(() => { middle.x = app.screen.width / 2; middle.y = app.screen.height / 2; crosshair.tint = view3d.raycast(middle, aim) ? 0xff4444 : 0xffffff; }); On a hit, aim.target is the node an event would go to, the same node as target3D. A raycast tests the same nodes that events do, so in a scene with nothing interactive it always misses.

The view's containsPoint returns true anywhere in its rectangle. That's why a click on empty space still reaches the view, and also why interactive 2D content behind the view never gets the pointer. There are three ways around this: Put the 2D content above the view in the display list. It draws on top, and a press on it never reaches the view or an OrbitCamera on it. Give the view a hitArea that covers only part of it. Outside that area, events reach what's behind the view. Set the view's eventMode to 'none' when its scene needs no pointer at all.
View3D and 2D content: converting between screen and world positions. Camera controls: the orbit and first-person controllers.

A Mesh3D's material decides how its surface looks: its colour, its textures, its opacity and how light shades it. Many meshes can share one material, such as every copy of a loaded model, and a change to it shows on all of them. Meshes shows how to change just one mesh, and Loading models shows how to give one model materials of its own.

Material Lighting Suits Material3D Physically based: how metallic and how rough it is Most lit surfaces, and the lit materials of glTF model files PhongMaterial A soft shade, plus a highlight you size and tint by eye Lit surfaces that needn't reflect their surroundings FlatMaterial None UI panels, icons, video screens, textures with lighting painted in const steel = new Material3D({ baseColor: 0xc8c8c8, metallic: 1, roughness: 0.3 }); const plastic = new PhongMaterial({ baseColor: 0x2f6f8b, shininess: 64 }); const screen = new FlatMaterial({ baseColorTexture: screenTexture }); Material3D is the usual choice. It's the only one of the three that reflects the view's environment, the sky and ground colours or the cube map that light the scene from all around, as Environment and IBL explains. PBR materials covers a Material3D's inputs and the light it needs. Physical extensions covers its option groups, each of which turns on one extra feature, such as clearcoat for a lacquer coat or transmission for glass. PhongMaterial does less work per pixel than Material3D. The view's environment gives it only soft light from all around, so it reflects nothing and its highlights come from direct lights alone. shininess sets the size of the highlight and specularColor sets its tint. PBR, Phong and flat puts the three materials side by side in one colour, and a slider in its pane sizes Phong's highlight. FlatMaterial does no lighting. It shows its colour and texture without any lights, and neither shadows nor the environment change it. Its mesh still casts a shadow, so set castShadow to false on a panel or screen that shouldn't cast one. The view's toneMapping, exposure and fog still reach it, so a tone-mapping curve shifts a flat material's colours too. A curve such as 'aces' squeezes bright light into the screen's range, as Tone mapping and exposure explains. To keep fog off a flat material, build it with fog set to false. @pixi/3d/extras adds ToonMaterial for cartoon shading. Toon and custom materials covers it and how to write a material of your own.

baseColor takes any PixiJS ColorSource, as a 2D tint does. It multiplies the base colour texture, so leave it white to show a texture unchanged. The material ignores the colour's own alpha. alpha sets the opacity instead, when the alpha mode allows it. baseColor and the other colour options take colours as a colour picker shows them. The engine converts them to linear light, where doubling a value doubles the light. Numbers you pass to a shader yourself skip that step, so convert a picked colour with srgbToLinear first. Geometry does this for vertex colours.

alphaMode decides what a material does with the alpha from alpha and from its textures: 'opaque', the default for the three materials above, ignores alpha, so setting alpha alone does nothing. An image's transparent pixels still draw, as a solid surface rather than holes. 'mask' throws away pixels whose alpha is below alphaCutoff and draws the rest solid. Use it for hard edges such as leaves, fences, grilles and cut-out sprites. 'blend' mixes the surface with what's behind it, in proportion to its alpha. Use it for fades, ghosts and soft edges. const leaves = new Material3D({ baseColorTexture: leafTexture, alphaMode: 'mask', doubleSided: true }); const ghost = new Material3D({ baseColor: 0x99ccff, alpha: 0.4, alphaMode: 'blend' }); A masked material draws with the opaque meshes, so it hides what's behind it and needs no sorting. A masked mesh's shadow doesn't show its holes yet, so turn off castShadow on one whose solid shadow would look wrong. Blended meshes draw after the opaque ones. Every frame the renderer sorts them from back to front by the distance from the camera to each mesh's origin, not by child order. It sorts each mesh as a whole, so a large blended mesh, or two that pass through each other, can draw in the wrong order where they overlap. A blended Mesh3D casts no shadow, as Shadows explains. Transparency switches two wordmark cards between the three modes, in front of a blended glass logo. With the cards on 'blend', walk round behind them and the draw order flips, so the logo draws over the cards. A solid material can switch to 'blend' for a fade and back to 'opaque' when the fade ends. For glass and water that bend what's behind them, use transmission instead.

By default a material draws only the front of each triangle, so an open surface such as a plane, a flag or a leaf card disappears when seen from behind. To draw both sides, build its material with doubleSided set to true, as the leaves above do. Lighting treats the back as if it faced the other way.

A material reads its textures from named slots in material.textures. All three materials above have a baseColor slot, which the baseColorTexture option fills. PhongMaterial and Material3D add more, such as normal, and Material3DTextures lists a Material3D's slots. Assign to a slot to swap its texture: brickMaterial.textures.baseColor = await Assets.load('bricks-wet.png'); Every mesh that uses the material shows the new texture. On a PlaneGeometry or a CubeGeometry an image appears upside down until you flip it. Geometry shows how. Each slot uses one of the GPU's texture inputs. Some devices allow only 16 per shader, and the engine uses a few of them itself. Most option groups take their slots whether or not you give them a texture, so leave out the groups a material doesn't use.

These options can't change once a material exists: On every material: doubleSided, flatShading, fog, topology, extraBits, and the per-pass overrides in its passes option. On a Material3D: which option groups it has, such as clearcoat, and whether its coat has a normal map or its anisotropy has a texture. On a PhongMaterial: whether it has a specularTexture or an emissive group. To change one, clone the material with the new value and assign the copy to the mesh's material. The copy keeps every other setting. mesh.material = mesh.material.clone({ doubleSided: true }); A clone can add a feature, such as an option group or an extra bit, but can't take one away. An option set to undefined keeps the material's value, and extraBits adds to the bits the material already has. To drop a feature, build a new material.

documents.t: A mesh picks up most changes to its material on the next frame: values such as baseColor and alpha, a texture swapped into a slot, and a switch to or from 'blend'. A few settings take effect only after you call invalidate on each mesh that uses the material. One is a field of state, which holds the material's depth, blending and culling settings. BaseMaterial3D lists the rest. // 'blend' draws the marker after the opaque walls, so it can draw over them const marker = new Mesh3D({ geometry, material: new FlatMaterial({ baseColor: 0xffcc00, alphaMode: 'blend' }) }); view3d.root.addChild(marker); // Later: show the marker through walls marker.material.state.depthTest = false; marker.invalidate(); A BatchedMesh3D slot is one of the meshes a batch draws. It needs its own invalidate call after more kinds of change, including a texture swap. Batched meshes shows which. A switch to or from 'blend' also needs setPassesAt.
